title: The OpenAI Coup: How a Nonprofit Board Could Fire Its CEO
dek: A 700-person company less than 5 years old, where a six-member nonprofit board exercised its power once and pulled off a coup — and its largest shareholder, Microsoft, isn't even on the board.
why: Luo Yihang has long been based in Silicon Valley and has had direct contact with Sam Altman. He lays out the full backstory of OpenAI's power structure and how Silicon Valley elite politics actually operates — this is not a retelling of the news.
who: Founders and investors watching AI corporate governance, founder control, and how overseas teams handle American-style politics; engineers who want to understand how OpenAI's board mechanism came to be.
skip: The 0:00-2:02 recap of the sequence of events at the start — skip it if you already know the news.

points.h: A 700-person company set off a global uproar
points.body: Luo Yihang judges this unprecedented: Twitter had internal chaos in its early years, but that stayed inside a small Silicon Valley circle and never got the whole world discussing it over popcorn. OpenAI had existed as a company for only a bit over 4 years, nearly 5, with a headcount of 700-plus, yet it caused this kind of storm — very rare. That contrast is itself the episode's central question: why could a single board vote at such a small company become a global event.

points.h: The means were political; the motive wasn't necessarily a conspiracy
points.body: Luo Yihang stresses repeatedly: the coup was extremely political, but political things don't necessarily have bad motives — political is a characteristic and a means. The real cause was still a fairly large divergence in philosophy — when GPTs and the GPTs Store launched on November 6, he personally was excited and shocked, feeling they had taken a very radical step. He also cautions that any decision, especially one by an outstanding figure, tends to mix very strong personal values with private interests, and the two can't be separated.

points.h: On safety, they say one thing and do another
points.body: In May of this year in Silicon Valley, Luo Yihang heard people in the circle say that Sam Altman actually says one thing and does another on alignment, safety and governance — that he is in fact very radical. This source is indirect, coming through an intermediary who is an AI entrepreneur, not someone inside OpenAI speaking directly. The contrast is with the three things Ilya has said in multiple interviews: his concern about whether AI can possess human love, his worries about superintelligence in relation to human ethical order and safety, and that the most important thing he pushed internally was alignment.

points.h: The most respected independent directors all left
points.body: The board list was originally long, 9 people, and they dropped out one after another: Elon Musk exited in '18 or '19 over a philosophical clash — at the time he opposed OpenAI becoming a nonprofit, and Luo Yihang believes that idea was genuine then; Elon Musk's ex-wife also exited a few months ago; most critically, LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman, whose reason for leaving was that he was preparing to do similar startups and investing. Luo Yihang says that if Reid Hoffman were still on the board, would this have been so hard to wind down in the end — because this person is especially constructive, and is good friends with many people whose relationships are otherwise deeply opposed. Of the three remaining, he feels ‘the people with prestige all left.’

points.h: They exercised power once, and it actually worked
points.body: Luo Yihang says two things shocked him. First, the company's key decisions were in fact all made by these three people; the directors were neither informed, nor had they fully exercised power in the past — and then they exercised power once, and it actually worked. Second, 700 people signed in support — does this company have internal strife at all? It's practically a solid block. He believes Ilya later joining the signatories was a very important trigger that got those 700-plus people to sign.

The mechanism was built like this: OpenAI started as a nonprofit, and the people on the board held no shares, only voting rights, representing the public in overseeing and managing the institution. In 2019 the situation changed — they were already doing training with the Transformer architecture, burning money badly, and the directors who had promised donations gave money without taking shares — Elon Musk promised 100 million, Reid Hoffman promised several hundred million, and the money came in bit by bit. So OpenAI Inc was set up as the nonprofit, and OpenAI LP as the limited-partnership for-profit vehicle to raise funding. The result: OpenAI LP has no board of its own — its board is the board of OpenAI Inc.

points.h: Microsoft holds 49% and isn't on the board
points.body: Microsoft changed enormously that year and settled on a line: AI goes toward artificial general intelligence, in partnership with OpenAI. Luo Yihang thinks this is connected to Qi Lu's departure — Qi Lu represented another, different line for AI inside Microsoft, one that at least didn't want to do AGI, and was more about industry applications. Microsoft invested all the way to today, and now holds 49% of OpenAI LP, just short of control, but neither Microsoft nor Satia himself is on the board, which is why they were only told at the end. Luo Yihang says this is something all of Silicon Valley had simply never encountered.

points.h: When things are this abnormal, something's up
points.body: Luo Yihang says he never thought this mechanism was good, from day one: the founder holds no shares, his voting power is on par with others, and a person who is nearly the largest shareholder has no voting rights — this is simply bizarre. He contrasts it with Silicon Valley's past, highly creative founder AB-share mechanism — Meta has so many outside shareholders that by equity they've already surpassed Zuckerberg, but Zuckerberg has AB voting rights to control the board. OpenAI instead went to the opposite extreme, moving toward greater dispersion in the name of a nonprofit. At the start of the year, when everyone reviewed it, they all thought this design was original and a key step in its success; as of today, everyone says this mechanism is deeply problematic.

points.h: YC once rejected founders for having an accent
points.body: In 2010, at a YC event at the Computer History Museum, Luo Yihang heard with his own ears Paul Graham tell an Eastern European founder one of the problems is that your English is not very good; the man said my English is really good, and Paul Graham replied you have a very strong accent. Luo Yihang says that person's accent was absolutely lighter than Satia's or Sundar Pichai's. He personally dislikes this, and considers an accent part of diversity. On Sam Altman you see none of this baggage or prejudice — in 2017, YC broke precedent by holding an event for Chinese LPs during the National Day holiday, complete with simultaneous interpretation.

points.h: He looks nerdy, but does the work of a super-connector
points.body: Luo Yihang says Sam Altman is simply another version of Silicon Valley's king of connections: he looks extremely nerdy, but all the work he does is the work people like Reid Hoffman do — convening groups, persuading people, asking for money, recruiting, presenting a vision. He has basically hardly ever done technology. Luo Yihang sees this as one of his traits: deep and broad connections, skilled at expressing and conveying a mission, skilled at fundraising, skilled at bringing different people together, and pushing things to happen in more radical ways.

points.h: He didn't write a tell-all; he talked about love
points.body: Luo Yihang thinks Sam Altman's handling over these days deserves praise: first, he didn't choose to write a tell-all or publicly go head-to-head, because that could damage his own image, force the other side to show many of their cards, and more importantly would hurt the organization; to date he hasn't revealed a single word externally about what the disagreement was or how the process went, nor has he publicly protested the unfairness. Second, he talked a lot about love, saying love the team. Third, he's become able to play the clown, with a lot of energy. Fourth, after Ilya tweeted that he regretted participation in the board, Sam Altman liked it with three hearts — Luo Yihang thinks this doesn't mean he fully agrees with every word Ilya said, but is a gesture to gather everyone back together.

points.h: Chinese aren't incapable — they were never taught
points.body: Luo Yihang says Chinese people feel somewhat out of place after arriving in Silicon Valley, because from childhood we were never educated to play these political games. Everyone complains that Indians form cliques, but he thinks this isn't clique-forming — Indians arrived in America earlier, and apart from accent they tolerated everything else well, and they know better how to find people to endorse them, platform them, support their positions, and defend their interests. White people do the same thing, it's just that no one calls them clique-forming. He gives Meta as an example: after '14 and '15 Chinese people grew more numerous, and especially after Chinese people reached VP level and above, Chinese at Meta began consciously doing similar things — mentoring and pulling people up, supporting their own, and actively saying that not all of us can be engineers, we need to be PMs and enter the business sector.

points.h: Silicon Valley truly favors these two types
points.body: Luo Yihang concludes that two types of people are especially welcomed by Silicon Valley, and behind this lies a very interesting tension. One is the white male who graduated from an Ivy League science and engineering school, with senior but not especially high-ranking experience at a big company — the easiest to win the favor of VCs and the environment, exemplified by Luminar founder Austin Russell: elite-school graduate, rich second generation, white, with a technological dream. The other is an ethnic-minority female immigrant like Mira Murati; Fei-Fei Li is also a typical example. But the former's cost of acquiring resources is far lower than the latter's: the white rich-kid elite-school type inherits the natural nourishment of this land, whereas Fei-Fei Li came at 16, couldn't understand classes when she entered high school, her parents went from practicing medicine to doing manual work, her mother got cancer, and she spent two years getting her English good enough to test into Stanford. Silicon Valley advertises itself as a paradise for the latter, but many people don't see the former's suppression of the latter.

terms.def: Making the machine's will and capabilities consistent with human will and capabilities — the core work Ilya pushed inside OpenAI.
A packaging image common among Silicon Valley CEOs: speaks softly, seems shy, doesn't like doing flashy, empty things.
Founders hold high-voting-power shares, so even if outside shareholders surpass them on equity they can still control the board; Meta is the typical example.
